rows.selection_reason: 1) Evidence/uncertainty: No experiments have been completed, so there is zero information about whether the data contains usable signal, how strong a simple baseline is, or which design axes (modality, profile, encoder, aggregation, fusion) will matter. 2) What this tests: config_001 (rna_only, singleprofile, pca_n2000) is the simplest possible configuration—single modality, single profile, a lightweight linear encoder, no aggregation or fusion. It establishes the performance floor and confirms whether the task is learnable at all with basic RNA features. 3) Why it is the best first use of budget: Starting from the minimal baseline gives every subsequent experiment a clean reference point. If config_001 performs reasonably, later experiments can isolate the marginal contribution of adding multiprofile, richer encoders (scvi, scgpt), image modality, or fusion. If it performs poorly, we learn early that representation quality is the critical bottleneck and can prioritize encoder choice before investing in fusion or aggregation. This maximizes information per experiment by anchoring the entire search to a well-understood reference, and it avoids the risk of interpreting a complex multimodal result without knowing what the simple components achieve.

With only one completed experiment (config_001: RNA-only, singleprofile, PCA → 48.5% acc), the most critical uncertainty is whether the image modality carries independent predictive signal for this task. config_010 (image_only, singleprofile, resnet50) is the cleanest parallel baseline: same profile setting, same simplicity level, but swapping the modality. If image-only performs comparably to RNA-only (~48%), multimodal fusion is unlikely to add much; if it substantially outperforms, the image channel is a strong signal source and multimodal fusion becomes a high-priority direction; if it underperforms, RNA remains the dominant modality and effort should focus on improving RNA representations (scvi, scgpt, multiprofile). This single experiment maximally reduces uncertainty about the core design question—whether to invest in multimodal fusion—before committing budget to more complex configurations that conflate multiple variables.

Evidence: RNA (pca_n2000, singleprofile) achieves 48.5% accuracy while image (resnet50) achieves only 20.8%, establishing RNA as the dominant signal modality. Uncertainty: We have no information on whether multiprofile aggregation improves the RNA representation, and this is the single most impactful untested design axis for the dominant modality. This experiment (config_002: rna_only, multiprofile, pca_n2000, avgpool) is a clean single-variable extension of config_001—only the profile setting changes from single to multi, with the simplest aggregation (avgpool)—isolating the effect of multi-profile aggregation on RNA performance. It is the best use of the next budget slot because: (1) it directly extends the strongest baseline, (2) it tests a fundamental data-structure question (does having multiple profiles help?) before committing to more complex choices like transformer aggregation or learned encoders, (3) if multiprofile helps, it opens a productive exploitation path (test transformer aggregation, then combine with better encoders); if it does not, it efficiently rules out that axis and redirects budget toward encoder choice. Testing multimodal fusion or image improvements before establishing the best RNA configuration would be premature given the large modality gap.

Evidence: The strongest result so far is config_002 (RNA-only, multiprofile, PCA, avgpool) at 0.591 acc, a ~10.6% improvement over the singleprofile baseline (config_001, 0.485). This confirms multiprofile aggregation is highly beneficial. Uncertainty: We do not yet know whether a transformer-based aggregation would further improve over simple average pooling, or whether avgpool is already near-optimal for this setup. This experiment (config_003) changes only the aggregation from avgpool to transformer while holding all other factors constant (RNA-only, multiprofile, PCA n2000), giving a clean isolation of the aggregation strategy. It is the best next step because it directly extends the best-performing configuration with a single-variable change, reducing uncertainty about a key design decision before investing budget in more complex choices (new encoders, multimodal fusion, or better image backbones).

Evidence: RNA dominates over image (0.485 vs 0.208), and within RNA, multi-profile + avgpool with PCA (config_002, acc 0.591) is clearly the best setup, beating both single-profile (0.485) and transformer aggregation (0.519). However, PCA is the only RNA encoder tested, so we cannot yet tell whether the learned representation quality is a bottleneck or whether the profile/aggregation design is the primary driver. Question: Does replacing PCA with the learned SCVI encoder (200-dim) improve performance when holding profile (multi) and aggregation (avgpool) fixed at their best-performing values? This isolates the encoder effect with a single-variable change from config_002. Why this is the best next experiment: It directly tests whether a more expressive RNA representation can push past the 0.591 ceiling, which determines whether subsequent multimodal experiments should pair a stronger encoder with image fusion. If SCVI matches or beats PCA, it justifies investing budget in multimodal configs with learned encoders; if it underperforms, PCA is sufficient and budget is better spent exploring fusion strategies. This is more informative than jumping to multimodal (where image's weakness confounds the fusion question) or testing image improvements (which seem unlikely to close the 0.38 gap to RNA).

Evidence: config_005 (scvi_n200, multiprofile, avgpool) is the current best at 0.650 acc, showing that learned encoders substantially outperform PCA (0.591) under the same profile/aggregation settings, and avgpool outperforms transformer for aggregation. Uncertainty: SCGPT is a completely untested encoder—we have zero data on how its learned representations compare to SCVI. Question tested: Does scgpt under the best-known settings (multiprofile, avgpool) match or exceed scvi_n200? This is a clean single-variable comparison to config_005 (only the RNA encoder changes). Why best next experiment: It reduces the most uncertainty by probing an entirely new encoder dimension under controlled conditions. The result directly determines which learned encoder to carry forward into any future multimodal or profile-setting experiments, making it more informative than re-testing aggregation (already strong evidence for avgpool) or jumping to multimodal (multiple simultaneous changes, and image alone was very weak at 0.208).

Evidence: scvi_n200 + multiprofile + avgpool (config_005, acc 0.650) is our strongest result, and for pca_n2000 multiprofile, avgpool clearly outperformed transformer (0.591 vs 0.519, config_002 vs config_003). However, scvi_n200 produces a fundamentally different (learned, nonlinear) representation than PCA, so the aggregation interaction may differ. Question: Does transformer aggregation help or hurt when paired with the scvi_n200 encoder, or does avgpool remain superior? Why this is the best next experiment: It is a clean single-variable comparison (aggregation only) that directly extends our best-performing configuration. The answer will determine the optimal aggregation strategy for all subsequent multimodal experiments involving scvi_n200, making it a high-information, low-risk choice that reduces uncertainty about a critical design axis before we commit budget to more complex multimodal configurations.

Evidence: RNA-only with scvi_n200/multiprofile/transformer is the current best (~0.653), while image-only with resnet50 is very weak (0.208). The critical uncertainty is whether the image modality has any useful signal at all, or whether the poor resnet50 result reflects a fundamental lack of image informativeness. config_013 (image_only, singleprofile, ViT-L) isolates the image encoder question by swapping resnet50 for a much stronger pretrained ViT-L while keeping everything else identical to config_010. This is a single-variable comparison that directly tells us whether image carries discriminative signal. If ViT-L is also weak, we can confidently rule out image and focus remaining budget on RNA-only refinement. If ViT-L is competitive, it justifies investing in multimodal fusion experiments (e.g., config_036/037). Without this prerequisite, any multimodal result would be confounded by not knowing whether the image branch contributes or dilutes the RNA signal.

Evidence: RNA-only models dominate (best: scvi_n200 + multiprofile + avgpool/transformer at ~0.65), while image-only models are very weak (ResNet50: 0.208, ViT-L: 0.227). The critical open question is whether the weak image signal provides any complementary information when fused with the strong RNA representation. This experiment pairs the best-validated RNA configuration (scvi_n200, multiprofile, avgpool) with the simplest image encoder (ResNet50) and simplest fusion (concat), forming a clean comparison against config_005 (0.650) and config_006 (0.653). If config_030 fails to exceed ~0.65, it strongly suggests image adds no value and we can eliminate all 36 multimodal configs, redirecting budget to RNA-only refinement. If it does exceed, it validates pursuing multimodal fusion and motivates testing weighted fusion and ViT-L. This is the highest-information experiment because it resolves the single most consequential design decision (unimodal vs. multimodal) with minimal confounding changes.

The key finding from config_030 (multimodal, scvi_n200, resnet50, avgpool, concat → 0.6315) is that the multimodal model underperforms the RNA-only counterpart (config_005: scvi_n200, multiprofile, avgpool → 0.6501). This is surprising and suggests the image modality or the fusion strategy is harmful. Config_031 is a clean single-variable comparison with config_030, changing only the fusion from concat to weighted. This directly tests whether the way modalities are combined is the bottleneck. If weighted fusion recovers the gap, the issue is feature interaction and we should explore fusion strategies further. If it does not, we gain strong evidence that resnet50 image features are net-negative for this task, redirecting the remaining budget toward optimizing the RNA-only pipeline (e.g., transformer aggregation with scvi_n200) rather than multimodal variants. Given the limited budget, isolating this one variable is more informative than jumping to a different image encoder or aggregation, which would confound multiple factors.
